The pace of AI development and adoption has been insanely fast compared to virtually every major technological revolution in history.

Rough estimate from 'invention' to 'widespread adoption':

* Automobiles: 1886 invention → 1920s mass adoption. ~40 years.

* Airplanes: 1903 first flight → 1950s mass commercial air travel. ~50 years.

* Plastics: 1907 Bakelite → 1950s widespread consumer applications. ~40+ years.

* Mobile phones: 1973 first handheld prototype → 2000 majority US adoption. 27 years.

* Personal Computers: ~1975 → 2000 majority US household ownership. ~25 years.

* Smartphones: 2007 iPhone → 2013 majority US adult adoption. 6 years.

* Chat GPT: ~3 years from GPT-2 "it kinda chats with you" to GPT-6 Astra "It's writing entire code bases"

Railroads, semiconductors, plastics, networking... the utility was there for all of them, and so was the potential profit.

These bubbles aren't about potential, they're about timing.

children.text: None of that matters when there is literally a 100x multiplier on efficiency because of batching. It's all a rounding error.

Be slightly careful with this. Large datacenters use power to operate the facility (this is measured as PUE > 1). Datacenter-oriented hardware often contains low-diameter, high static pressure fans that consume quite impressive amounts of power that are not counted as overhead in the PUE calculation.

A home- or office-oriented workstation will have much less power-hungry fans (go compare a Noctua datasheet to a server fan datasheet - the Noctua wipes the floor with a server fan if measured by CFM/W, and the internal temperature rise is mostly controlled by airflow and not by static pressure). And in some climates and times of year the marginal facility HVAC cost associated with running a computer may be zero or even negative.

And lower utilization hardware may run in on a more efficient point on the power-vs-performance curve. [0]

That being said, your overall point is correct.

[0] For a dramatic demonstration of how much this curve matters, you can run a non-CPU-saturating, non-latency-sensitive workload on various Intel CPUs with and without turbo on. Seeing a 2x or greater difference in reported power is quite possible. (Intel is terribly at writing platform firmware and the default behavior may be wildly suboptimal.)

Large data centers are dramatically more efficient at utilizing both the power and the hardware.

At it's core, running a top-tier LLM means linear load of trillion+ weights from RAM for every token. The cost of this operation absolutely dwarfs the cost of doing the actual math. If you are only serving a single user, you can only amortize this over a handful of token streams, times like 2-4 for speculative decoding. If you are running in a datacenter, you can batch thousands of streams, and get correspondingly much more tokens out of the same expenditure of energy and hardware.

Interesting... Upon reflection, I feel like it's a "yes, and" proposition coming down to failure mode.

[Type A] Constant use a constant power level: Quantum world rules would dominate.

When run hot, electron tunneling will kill off individual transistors, and AFAIK that is a cascading failure mode once it takes root. A big enough failed spot, even if localised, could effectively kill a core (if not the whole chip---too many errors). A local hotspot will directly affect neighbours, and indirectly the chip as a whole because the same work is being pushed on fewer cores.

[Type B] Thermal cycled: Mechanical and electrical factors would dominate...

Microfractures / mechanical damage in weak areas of whole chips, and motherboards. In a hyperscaler server rack, if a board dies that part of the rack is dead---micro-maintenance is probably too expensive.

And speculating further, it stands to reason that Type B failures would likely cause Type A failures, and vice-versa.

I suspect GPU and CPU failure rates have more to do with stress from thermal cycling, if they can keep them loaded and running without heating/cooling cycles, they should last pretty long. Their lifetime is probably dictated more from when do they stop being competitive on a flop/watt basis than by their failure rate.
